newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany's Waigel keeps up hard line on EMU targets.
newsitem.headline: Germany's Waigel keeps up hard line on EMU targets.

text.p: Germany will meet the fiscal goals for European currency union membership without seeking any softening of the criteria or using accounting tricks, Finance Minister Theo Waigel said on Sunday.
"The German finance minister will spare no effort in meeting the criteria," Waigel said in an interview with the Frankfurter Allgemeine Sonntagszeitung.
EU members are scheduled to decide in early 1998 which countries will be in the first wave of monetary union, due to begin in 1999. Their decision will be based on data for 1997.
Waigel's tough stance contrasts with growing anxieties among the German public on the planned single currency and scepticism among pundits on Germany's ability to meet the targets.

A poll in an advance copy of the news magazine Spiegel says that 77 percent of Germans want EMU to be postponed from the 199 start date, the latest in a series of polls which show increasing German anxiety about the planned single currency.

A report in Monday's edition of the news magazine Focus cited experts at the Finance Ministry saying that Germany would not meet the target for debt-to-GDP ratio of 60 percent, and that in 1997 61.5 percent was more likely.
A spokeswoman for the Finance Ministry said it was too early to comment on the final outturn for the debt-to-GDP ratio and said the government would be doing everything it could to meet the criteria.
A former Bundesbank member, Wilhelm Noelling, threatened to lodge a legal challenge to the German government if Germany went ahead with EMU while missing strict entry criteria.
In Britain's Financial Mail on Sunday newspaper, Noelling called for EMU to be postponed saying he believed not even Germany would meet the entry criteria.
Waigel, however, remains confident of Germany's chances of meeting the criteria and said it will do so without any softening of the entry criteria.
Germany will adhere to the requirement for would-be members to cut budget deficits down to or below three percent of gross domestic product by year end.

"Three is three. We have developed our budgetary concept in such a way, and agreed this with th e different states and local authorities, so that the deficit in 1997 will be three percent of GDP," Waigel said.
The Maastricht Treaty contained powerful policies for establishing stability in currency union, he said.

The statute establishing the European Central Bank, which will be set up in Frankfurt in 1998, was clearly oriented towards stability and had given the ECB a stronger status than even the powerful German Bundesbank, he said.
"The treaty contains sensible economic criteria. With these we have succeeded in establishing a culture of stability which no one in Europe would have thought possible 10 years ago."

The daily newspaper Bild on Saturday quoted Waigel as telling the parliamentary budget committee: "When it comes to meeting the Maastricht criteria, then crediting German payments to the EU must also be discussed."
A ministry spokeswoman said the report was wrong, adding that Waigel had merely pointed out to the committee the heavy burden placed on Germany through its big payments to the EU.
"We're not pulling any tricks," the spokeswoman said.

European Commission President Jacques Santer also takes a hard line on meeting the criteria. Santer said on Saturday it was vital that the criteria for EMU membership laid out in the Maastricht Treaty should be strictly adhered to.
He dismissed calls to delay the planned 1999 EMU start date. "I am worried that if we delay the start date now, we will delay currency union for a whole generation," Santer said.
